source.title: Geometry of Reason: Spectral Signatures of Valid Mathematical Reasoning

record.tranche_reason: The paper mentions induction heads and reports an abstract-level ablation claim, but does not test any of the specified induction-mechanism, training-transition, in-context-learning, universality, or data-dependence versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many results about attention spectra and mathematical-proof validity. Those do not measure induction behavior or in-context learning and are not included as rows. The abstract says causal ablation links the spectral signature to induction-head circuits, but the text gives no ablation details or specific measurements.
record.test_reason: The study analyses spectral features of attention graphs to classify mathematical-proof validity. It never measures induction behaviour, previous-token composition, in-context learning or training dynamics. Induction heads appear only in a Related Work citation of Olsson et al. and in one abstract sentence asserting causal ablation. The body contains no ablation and the Limitations call the method 'diagnostic, not causal'. Its results do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that training-free spectral features of attention graphs (HFER, Fiedler value, smoothness, entropy) separate valid from invalid Lean proofs across seven models (d up to 3.30). They add that the signal tracks logical rather than compiler validity, and that attention design (sliding-window attention) changes which feature carries the signal. The abstract's induction-head ablation claim is unsupported in the body, which states the method is 'diagnostic, not causal'.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes attention graphs and spectral features for mathematical-proof validity; it does not reproduce the original induction-head or training-transition methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported proof-validity signal varies by architecture and metric; for example, the paper reports that Sliding Window Attention shifts the strongest feature from HFER to smoothness. This does not establish sensitivity of induction behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: The abstract asserts that causal ablation links the proof-validity spectral signature to induction-head circuits. The body reports no ablation, and the Limitations call the method correlational.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction-head circuits contribute to attention spectral signatures of valid formal reasoning (unsubstantiated in text).

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The only induction-head-related result is a brief abstract statement; the text provides no ablation procedure, model or circuit details, baseline, numerical outcome, or uncertainty for it.
record.rows_left_out: Spectral classification results, model comparisons, and proof-validity controls were left out because they do not measure induction behavior or in-context learning.

Not tested: the cross-family results concern a proof-validity spectral signal, not induction heads.

Not tested: no few-shot task-learning attribution.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. Induction heads are mentioned only via a citation and one unsupported abstract sentence. No result in the paper bears on any version of the claim.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test formation in small attention-only transformers, composition with a previous-token head, or [A][B] copying.
Does not track induction-head formation, in-context learning, or training loss over training time.
Does not measure induction heads as a mechanism for most in-context learning in large transformers.
Cross-model spectral results concern proof validity, not the presence of induction behavior across model families, sizes, runs, architectures, or modalities.
Does not vary training data or training setup to test induction-head formation or persistence of in-context learning.
Does not compare induction heads with other mechanisms as carriers of few-shot task learning.
Does not study the timing or sequence of induction-head formation.

rows.check: This is not a result. It is an unsupported abstract assertion: no ablation procedure, model, circuit, baseline or number appears anywhere in the text. The 'observed' state is unwarranted, and the Limitations section ('Diagnostic, not causal') contradicts the claim. The row should be dropped or kept only as a note.

relation.reason: Besides citing Olsson et al. in Related Work, the abstract makes its own unsupported causal assertion about induction-head circuits. This exceeds citation alone but supplies no documented test.

tranche.reason: Proof-validity spectral diagnostics neither test an induction-head claim version nor use an established induction-head mechanism as a tool.

source_check.notes: Spectral-feature universality across models is not evidence of induction-head universality. R1 belongs among unsupported assertions, not experimental evidence for any claim version.

statements.correction: Abstract: causal induction-head attribution asserted. Section 4.4 and Appendix C: robustness ablations reported. Section 8: method described as correlational; mechanistic explanation left to future work. No causal induction-head ablation documented.
statements.problem: The abstract assertion and correlational limitation are correctly identified. However, saying the body reports no ablation is too broad: it reports robustness ablations, though no causal induction-head ablation.
